questions.question_text:
(a) Find the first four terms, in ascending powers of x, of the binomial expansion of (1 + 8x)^(1/2), giving each term in simplest form. (3)
(b) Explain how you could use x = 1/32 in the expansion to find an approximation for sqrt(5). There is no need to carry out the calculation. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts the binomial expansion with n = 1/2 and obtains the correct structure for term 3 or term 4 (correct coefficient with the correct power of x; do not accept nCr notation for coefficients). A1: Correct (unsimplified) expression - may be implied by the correct simplified expression. A1: 1 + 4x - 8x^2 + 32x^3 (award even if there are extra terms, or if the terms are listed separately as 1, 4x, -8x^2, 32x^3). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Substitutes x = 1/32 into (1+8x)^(1/2) to obtain 5/4 or an equivalent such as sqrt(5)/2 (also implied by sqrt(5)/2 = 1145/1024 for a correct expansion; alternatively substitutes x=1/32 into both sides and makes a connection between the two sides using = or ~=). It is not enough to just state 'substitute x=1/32 into the expansion' or into just the RHS '1+4x-8x^2+32x^3'. A1ft: Requires a full and correct explanation of how the expansion can be used to estimate sqrt(5), e.g. calculates 1 + 4*(1/32) - 8*(1/32)^2 + 32*(1/32)^3 and multiplies the result by 2 (this can be scored from an incorrect binomial expansion, or one with more terms; the explanation can be purely mathematical, e.g. sqrt(5)/2 = 1145/1024 => sqrt(5) = 1145/512 is acceptable). SC: For 1 mark, M1 A0 is scored for a statement such as 'substitute x=1/32 into both sides of part (a) and make sqrt(5) the subject'. (2 marks)

questions.question_text: By taking logarithms of both sides, solve the equation 4^(3p-1) = 5^210, giving the value of p to one decimal place. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Takes logs of both sides and uses the power law on each side (condone a missing bracket on the lhs and slips; award for any base including ln, but the logs must be the same base on both sides, e.g. (3p-1)log4 = 210log5). dM1: A full method leading to a value for p, dependent on the previous M mark, with an attempt to change the subject of the equation in the correct order: 3p = 210log5/log4 + 1 => p = ... (condoning slips; numerical versions are also acceptable, e.g. (3p-1)*0.60 = 210*0.7 => 1.8p-0.6=147 => p=82; using incorrect log laws, e.g. (3p-1)log4 = 210log5 => 3p = 210log(4/5) +/- 1, scores dM0). A1: p = awrt 81.6 following a correct method (a correct answer with no working scores 0 marks, since the question demands the method). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Relative to a fixed origin O, point A has position vector 2i + 5j - 6k, point B has position vector 3i - 3j - 4k, point C has position vector 2i - 16j + 4k.
(a) Find vector AB. (2)
(b) Show that quadrilateral OABC is a trapezium, giving reasons for your answer. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to subtract either way round (if no method is seen, implied by two of +-1i +-8j +-2k correct). A1: AB = i - 8j + 2k (not the coordinate form (1,-8,2)). (2 marks)
(b) M1: Compares their i-8j+2k with OC = 2i-16j+4k by stating any one of: OC = 2*AB, or (2,-16,4) = 2*(1,-8,2), or OC = lambda*AB (or vice versa); may be awarded even if AB was subtracted 'the wrong way round' or if there was one numerical slip. A1: A full explanation as to why OABC is a trapezium - requires the fully correct AB = i-8j+2k from part (a), and needs a stated reason plus a minimal conclusion, e.g. 'OC = 2*AB, therefore OC is parallel to AB, so OABC is a trapezium' (accept either definition of trapezium - one pair, or only one pair, of parallel sides; calculations relating to sides OA and CB can be ignored even if incorrect). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
The function f is defined by f(x) = (3x-7)/(x-2), x != 2.
(a) Find f^(-1)(7). (2)
(b) Show that ff(x) = (ax+b)/(x-3) where a and b are integers to be found. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Either attempts to solve (3x-7)/(x-2) = 7 => x = ... (look for an attempt to multiply by (x-2) leading to a value for x), or attempts f^(-1)(x) [which is (2x-7)/(x-3)] and substitutes x=7 (the method for finding f^(-1)(x) should be sound, but slips can be condoned). A1: 7/4 oe. (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to fully substitute (3x-7)/(x-2) into f(x); condone slips, but the expression must have a correct form, e.g. [3*((3x-7)/(x-2)) - 7] / [(3x-7)/(x-2) - 2]. dM1: Attempts to multiply all terms on the numerator and denominator by (x-2) to create a fraction where both the numerator P(x) and denominator Q(x) are linear expressions, via careful and accurate work; implied by reaching a=2, b=-7 following correct work (methods using (3x-7)/(x-2) = a + b/(x-2) can be scored in a similar way). A1: Reaches ff(x) = (2x-7)/(x-3). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
A car has six forward gears. The fastest speed of the car in 1st gear is 28 km/h; in 6th gear is 115 km/h. Given that the fastest speed of the car in successive gears is modelled by an arithmetic sequence, (a) find the fastest speed of the car in 3rd gear. (3)
Given that the fastest speed of the car in successive gears is modelled by a geometric sequence, (b) find the fastest speed of the car in 5th gear. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Translates the problem into maths using nth term = a + (n-1)d and attempts to find d: look for either 115 = 28 + 5d => d = ..., or an attempt at (115-28)/5, condoning slips (implied by use of d=17.4; note 115=28+6d=>d=... is M0). M1: Uses the model to find the fastest speed in 3rd gear using 28 + 2*'d' or equivalent (can be awarded following an incorrect 'd'). A1: 62.8 km/h (lack of units condoned; exact equivalents such as 314/5 allowed). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Translates the problem into maths using nth term = a*r^(n-1) and attempts to find r, using the 1st and 6th gear (not the 3rd gear from part (a)): look for either 115=28r^5 => r=... oe, or the 5th root of (115/28), condoning slips (implied by r=awrt 1.33). M1: Uses the model to find the fastest speed in 5th gear using 28*'r'^4 or 115/'r' oe (can be awarded following an incorrect 'r'; a common misread is finding 3rd gear as in (a) - if clear what was done, e.g. u3=28*'r'^2, this mark can still be awarded). A1: awrt 86.7 km/h (lack of units condoned; expressions must be evaluated). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Express sin x + 2 cos x in the form R sin(x + alpha) where R and alpha are constants, R > 0 and 0 < alpha < pi/2. Give the exact value of R and give the value of alpha in radians to 3 decimal places. (3)
The temperature, theta °C, inside a room on a given day is modelled by the equation theta = 5 + sin(pi*t/12 - 3) + 2*cos(pi*t/12 - 3),  0 <= t < 24, where t is the number of hours after midnight. Using the equation of the model and your answer to part (a),
(b) deduce the maximum temperature of the room during this day. (1)
(c) find the time of day when the maximum temperature occurs, giving your answer to the nearest minute. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: R = sqrt(5) (exact). M1: Proceeds to a value of alpha from tan(alpha) = 2, or sin(alpha) = 2/R, or cos(alpha) = 1/R (implied by either awrt 1.11 radians or 63.4 degrees). A1: alpha = awrt 1.107. (3 marks)
(b) B1ft: Deduces that the maximum temperature is (5 + sqrt(5)) °C or awrt 7.24 °C (remember to isw; condone a lack of units; follow through on their value of R, allowing (5 + 'R') °C). (1 mark)
(c) M1: A complete strategy to find t from pi*t/12 + 1.107 - 3 = pi/2 (follow through on their 1.107, but the angle must be in radians; a degrees-based method is possible using 15t + 63.4 - 171.9 = 90). A1: awrt t = 13.2. A1: Gives the time of day correctly - accept 13:14, 1:14 pm, 13 hours 14 minutes after midnight, 13h 14, or 1 hour 14 minutes after midday (if in doubt, send to review). (3 marks)
Note: it is possible to attempt (b) and (c) via differentiation, e.g. d(theta)/dt = (pi/12)*[cos(pi*t/12-3) - 2*sin(pi*t/12-3)] = 0 => tan(pi*t/12-3) = 1/2 => t = 13.23 = 13:14 scores M1 A1 A1 (a version with a coefficient slip, e.g. missing the factor of 2 inside the sine term, can score M1 A0 A1 as a special case). A value of t = 1.23 implies the minimum has been found, so is an incorrect method (M0).
questions.notes: The raw OCR text lost square-root symbols throughout this question (a common artefact in this dataset). 'R = 5' in the mark scheme, and '(5 + 5) °C' for the deduced maximum temperature, have been reconstructed as 'R = sqrt(5)' and '(5 + sqrt(5)) °C' respectively - this is confirmed by the numeric check 5 + sqrt(5) = 7.236, which matches the mark scheme's stated alternative 'awrt 7.24 °C'.

questions.question_text: Figure 1 shows a sketch of a curve C with equation y = f(x) and a straight line l. The curve C meets l at the points (-2, 13) and (0, 25). The shaded region R is bounded by C and l. Given that f(x) is a quadratic function in x, and (-2, 13) is the minimum turning point of y = f(x), use inequalities to define R. (5)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Attempts the equation of the line, e.g. substitutes (-2,13) into y = mx + 25 and finds m. A1: Equation of l is y = 6x + 25. M1: Attempts the equation of curve C, e.g. attempts to use the point (0,25) within y = a(x+2)^2 + 13 to find a (an alternative is to set up and solve simultaneous equations in a and b using y=ax^2+bx+25, the point (-2,13), and gradient 0 at x=-2). A1: Equation of C is y = 3(x+2)^2 + 13, or y = 3x^2 + 12x + 25. B1ft: Region R is fully defined by 3(x+2)^2 + 13 < y < 6x + 25 oe, following through on their equations for l and C (strict or non-strict inequalities are allowed if used consistently; the inequalities may be given separately or in set notation; if there are multiple solutions, mark the final one). (5 marks)
questions.notes: This question is about finding the equation of a straight line and of a quadratic curve (from its minimum turning point and y-intercept) and then defining a shaded region between them using inequalities. It is not circle geometry (the fixed topic vocabulary's 'coordinate-geometry' tag is specifically for circles), and it does not cleanly fit any other topic in the given 16-item vocabulary either (it is not 'differentiation' - no calculus is used to find the vertex, it's given directly - and it is not 'functions' in the composite/inverse/domain-range sense). Tagging as 'coordinate-geometry' per the task instructions' guidance for surfacing gaps rather than silently dropping the question, but flagging this as a genuine vocabulary gap: quadratic-curve-plus-line region problems have no clean home in the current 16 topics.

questions.question_text: A new smartphone was released by a company. The company monitored the total number of phones sold, n, at time t days after the phone was released. The company observed that, during this time, the rate of increase of n was proportional to n. Use this information to write down a suitable equation for n in terms of t. (You do not need to evaluate any unknown constants in your equation.) (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Any equation of the correct form, involving n and an exponential in t, e.g. n = e^(+-t), n = A*e^(+-t), n = A*e^(kt) where A and k are positive constants (condone n = A + B*e^(kt); condone an intermediate unrearranged form such as ln(n) = kt + c, or ln(n) = kt). A1: e.g. n = A*e^(kt), n = e^(kt+c), n = e^(kt)*e^(c) (there is no requirement to state that A and k are positive constants, but the two constants must be different - mark the final answer, so n = e^(kt+c) followed by n = e^(kt) + e^(c) is M1 A0). Versions without 'e' are also acceptable, e.g. n = A*k^t, marked using the same criteria. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 2 shows a sketch of the curve C with equation y = f(x) where f(x) = 4(x^2 - 2)*e^(-2x), x in R.
(a) Show that f'(x) = 8(2 + x - x^2)*e^(-2x). (3)
(b) Hence find, in simplest form, the exact coordinates of the stationary points of C. (3)
The function g and the function h are defined by g(x) = 2f(x), x in R; h(x) = 2f(x) - 3, x >= 0.
(c) Find (i) the range of g, (ii) the range of h. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts the product rule and uses e^(-2x) -> k*e^(-2x), k != 0 (if u=4(x^2-2), v=e^(-2x) are stated with u'=..., v'=...e^(-2x), it can be implied by their vu'+uv'; if written down without working, award for f'(x) = p*x*e^(-2x) +- q(x^2-2)*e^(-2x); the quotient rule route via f(x)=4(x^2-2)/e^(2x) is also acceptable). A1: A correct f'(x), which may be unsimplified. A1*: Proceeds correctly to the given answer f'(x) = 8(2+x-x^2)*e^(-2x), showing all necessary steps with no errors and correct bracketing (a move from the simplified unfactorised f'(x) = 8x*e^(-2x) - 8(x^2-2)*e^(-2x) to the given answer in one step is allowed, but not from an unsimplified 4*2x*e^(-2x) + 4(x^2-2)*(-2e^(-2x))). (3 marks)
(b) B1: States or implies x = -1, 2 as the roots of f'(x) = 0. M1: Substitutes one x value into f(x) to find a y value (decimals to 3sf are allowed; may be scored from work in part (c) if only x-coordinates are stated here). A1: Obtains (-1, -4e^2) and (2, 8e^-4) as the stationary points (must be scored in (b); remember to isw; extra solutions e.g. from x=0 are penalised on this mark). (3 marks)
(c)(i) B1ft: For a correct range written using correct notation, e.g. g(x) >= -8e^2, or {y : y >= -8e^2}, following through on 2 times their minimum y-value from part (b), provided it is negative (condone a decimal answer consistent with (b) to 3sf or better). (1 mark)
(c)(ii) M1: Either attempts 2f(0) - 3 = 2*(-8) - 3 = -19 and identifies this as the lower bound, or attempts 2*their '8e^-4' - 3 and identifies this as the upper bound. A1: Range -19 <= y <= 16e^-4 - 3, oe, but must be exact. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Use the substitution x = u^2 + 1 to show that the integral from x=5 to x=10 of 3/[(x-1)(3 + 2*sqrt(x-1))] dx equals the integral from u=p to u=q of 6/[u(3+2u)] du, where p and q are positive constants to be found. (4)
(b) Hence, using algebraic integration, show that the integral from x=5 to x=10 of 3/[(x-1)(3 + 2*sqrt(x-1))] dx = ln(a), where a is a rational constant to be found. (6)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
Notes: mark (a) and (b) together as one complete question.
(a) B1: x = u^2+1 => dx = 2u du oe. M1: Attempts a full substitution of x = u^2+1, including dx -> 2u du, to form an integrand in terms of u (condone slips, but there must be an attempt to use the correct substitution on the denominator). B1: Finds the correct limits, either states p=2, q=3, or shows sight of the embedded values as limits to the integral. A1*: Clear reasoning including one fully correct intermediate line, including the integral signs, leading to the given expression, ignoring limits (so B1, M1, B0, A1 is possible if the limits are incorrect, omitted, or left as 5 and 10). (4 marks)
(b) M1: Uses the correct form of partial fractions 6/[u(3+2u)] = A/u + B/(3+2u), leading to values of A and B (not scored for just quoting correct values of A and B). A1: Correct partial fractions 6/[u(3+2u)] = 2/u - 4/(3+2u). dM1: An overall problem-solving mark for using the correct PF form and integrating using logs - look for P*ln(u) + Q*ln(3+2u). A1ft: Correct integration for their A/u + B/(3+2u) -> A*ln(u) + (B/2)*ln(3+2u), with or without modulus signs. M1: Uses their 2 and 3 as limits, with at least one correct application of the addition or subtraction law of logs, leading to the form k*ln(b) or ln(a) (partial fractions must have been attempted; condone bracketing slips; alternatively changing the u's back to x's and using limits of 5 and 10). A1: Proceeds to ln(49/36) (answers without working should be sent to review). (6 marks)

questions.question_text:
Circle C1 has equation x^2 + y^2 = 100. Circle C2 has equation (x-15)^2 + y^2 = 40. The circles meet at points A and B (Figure 3).
(a) Show that angle AOB = 0.635 radians to 3 significant figures, where O is the origin. (4)
The region shown shaded in Figure 3 is bounded by C1 and C2.
(b) Find the perimeter of the shaded region, giving your answer to one decimal place. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: For the key step in an attempt to find either coordinate of where the two circles meet - sets up an equation in a single variable, e.g. (x-15)^2 + 100 - x^2 = 40 => x = ..., leading to a value for x or y. A1: x = 9.5 (or y = sqrt(39)/2 = awrt +-3.12). M1: Uses the radius of circle C1 and correct trigonometry to find angle AOB, e.g. attempts cos(alpha) = 9.5/10 to find alpha then doubles it (alternatives include tan(alpha) = sqrt(100-9.5^2)/9.5, or the cosine rule cos(AOB) = (10^2+10^2-39/4)/(2*10*10) = 161/200). A1*: Correct and careful work proceeding to the given answer, angle AOB = 2*arccos(9.5/10) = 0.635 rad (3sf); condone an answer given to greater accuracy, or a truncated intermediate value provided the trig equation used is correct, or a solution written down directly from awrt 36.4 degrees. An equivalent method finds all three lengths of triangle OAX (X on the line joining the centres) then applies the cosine rule to find alpha before doubling it. (4 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to use the arc length formula s = r*theta with r = 10 and theta = 2*pi - 0.635 (may be embedded within a combined expression, e.g. 10*2*pi + 40*2*pi - 10*0.635, which is fine for this mark). M1: Attempts a correct method to find angle AXB or AXO in circle C2 (X being the centre of C2), e.g. cos(beta) = (15-9.5)/sqrt(40) => beta = ... (note angle AXB = 1.03 rad), or an equivalent using tan(beta) or the cosine rule in triangle AXB (many candidates incorrectly believe this angle to be 0.635, which scores M0 dM0 A0). dM1: A full and complete attempt to find the perimeter of the region by summing the two arc lengths, e.g. attempts 10*(2*pi - 0.635) + sqrt(40)*(2*pi - 2*beta) (dependent on having scored both preceding M marks). A1: awrt 89.7. (4 marks)
questions.notes: The raw OCR text lost square-root symbols again here: the radius of C2 (sqrt(40)) appears in the raw mark scheme simply as '40', and the formula for angle beta shows a division by '40' rather than 'sqrt(40)'. Both have been reconstructed as sqrt(40), confirmed by the numeric check: 10*(2*pi-0.635) + sqrt(40)*(2*pi-2*0.515) = 56.48 + 33.23 = 89.71, matching the mark scheme's stated answer 'awrt 89.7'.

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
(a) Show that cosec(theta) - sin(theta) = cos(theta)*cot(theta), theta != (180n)°, n is an integer. (3)
(b) Hence, or otherwise, solve for 0 < x < 180°: cosec(x) - sin(x) = cos(x)*cot(3x - 50°). (5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States or uses cosec(theta) = 1/sin(theta) (do not accept with the theta missing). M1: For the key step of forming a single fraction/common denominator, e.g. cosec(theta) - sin(theta) = 1/sin(theta) - sin(theta) = [1 - sin^2(theta)]/sin(theta) (allow if written as 1/sin(theta) - sin^2(theta)/sin(theta); condone missing variables for this mark). A1*: Shows careful work with all necessary steps to cos^2(theta)/sin(theta) = cos(theta) * [cos(theta)/sin(theta)] = cos(theta)*cot(theta), the given answer, with no notational or bracketing errors. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Uses part (a), cancels or factorises out the cos(x) term, to establish that one solution is found when x = 3x - 50° (solutions via cot(A) - cot(B) = 0 => cot(A-B) = 0, or tan(A) - tan(B) = 0 => tan(A-B) = 0, are acceptable as long as the false general identity cot(A)-cot(B)=cot(A-B) is not explicitly stated). A1: x = 25°. M1: For the key step of realising that cot(x) has a period of 180°, and finding a second solution by solving x + 180° = 3x - 50° (sight of x=115° can imply this mark, provided the step x=3x-50° has been seen; using reciprocal functions, it is for realising tan(x) has period 180°). A1: x = 115° (withhold if there are additional values in the range (0,180), but ignore values outside the range). B1: Deduces that a further solution can be found from cos(x) = 0 => x = 90° (ignore additional values here). (5 marks)
Note: alternative approaches (working right-to-left, working on both sides simultaneously, or converting to sin(3x-50°-x)=0 for part (b)) score the same mark allocation for equivalent steps.

questions.question_text:
A sequence of numbers a1, a2, a3, ... is defined by a_(n+1) = k(a_n + 2)/a_n, n is a positive integer, where k is a constant. Given that the sequence is a periodic sequence of order 3, and a1 = 2,
(a) show that k^2 + k - 2 = 0. (3)
(b) For this sequence explain why k != 1. (1)
(c) Find the value of the sum from r=1 to 80 of a_r. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Applies the sequence formula a_(n+1) = k(a_n+2)/a_n once, seen in an attempt to find the second term, e.g. a2 = k(2+2)/2 = 2k. M1: Attempts to find a1 through a4 and sets a4 = a1 (condone slips; alternatively sets a4=2, works backwards to find a3, and equates to k+1; there is no requirement to see the labels, or to simplify the terms, but the correct terms must appear in the correct order). FYI: a1=2, a2=2k, a3=k+1, a4=k(k+3)/(k+1), so 2 = k(k+3)/(k+1). A1*: Proceeds to the given answer k^2+k-2=0 with accurate work showing all necessary lines. (3 marks)
(b) B1: States that when k=1, all terms are the same (equal to 2), and concludes that the sequence does not have a period of order 3 (do not accept vague statements like 'the terms just repeat' or 'it would mean all the terms of the sequence are 2' with no reference to order 3; accepting 'it has order 1' is fine). (1 mark)
(c) B1: Deduces the repeating terms are a1=a4=2, a2=a5=-4, a3=a6=-1 (using k=-2, the root of k^2+k-2=0 other than k=1). M1: Uses a clear strategy to find the sum to 80 terms, usually via multiples of the first three terms, e.g. sum = 26*(2 + -4 + -1) + a79 + a80 = 26*(2-4-1) + 2 + -4, or 27*(2-4-1) - a81 = 27*(2-4-1) - (-1) (candidates working in terms of k score this for 27*2 + 27*(2k) + 26*(k+1), or 80k+80). A1: -80. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
A large spherical balloon is deflating. At time t seconds the balloon has radius r cm and volume V cm^3. The volume of the balloon is modelled as decreasing at a constant rate.
(a) Using this model, show that dr/dt = -k/r^2, where k is a positive constant. (3)
Given that the initial radius of the balloon is 40 cm, after 5 seconds the radius of the balloon is 20 cm, and the volume of the balloon continues to decrease at a constant rate until the balloon is empty,
(b) solve the differential equation to find a complete equation linking r and t. (5)
(c) Find the limitation on the values of t for which the equation in part (b) is valid. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Uses the model to state dV/dt = -c for a positive constant c (any letter is acceptable including k; note dV/dt = c is B0 unless c is stated to be a negative constant). M1: For an attempt to use dV/dt = dV/dr * dr/dt with their dV/dt = -c and dV/dr = 4*pi*r^2 (any constant coefficient for dV/dr is fine - there is no requirement to use the correct sphere volume formula for this mark). A1*: Proceeds to the given answer with an intermediate line equivalent to dr/dt = -c/(4*pi*r^2), replacing the constant c/(4*pi) with k (if the candidate started with dV/dt = -k, a minimal explanation of why k/(4*pi) is itself a constant, so can be relabelled k, is required). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Separates the variables correctly, integral of r^2 dr = integral of -k dt, and integrates one side with at least one index correct (integral signs need not be seen). A1: Correct integration, r^3/3 = -kt (+alpha) or equivalent (the +alpha is not required for this mark; may be awarded if k has already been given a numerical value). M1: Uses the initial condition t=0, r=40 to find a value for the constant of integration alpha = 64000/3. M1: Uses the second condition t=5, r=20, and their alpha, to find k (may be awarded even if the equation has been adapted incorrectly, e.g. each term cube-rooted). A1: Obtains a correct equation for the model, e.g. r^3 = 64000 - 11200t, or an exact equivalent (isw after a correct answer is seen; condone recurring decimals such as 21333.3 for 64000/3, but not rounded/truncated decimals). (5 marks)
(c) M1: Recognises that the model is only valid while r >= 0 (condone r>0), and uses this to find t, e.g. by setting the RHS of the model equation to 0 and solving for t. A1ft: States that the model is valid for times up to and including 40/7 seconds (allow t < 40/7 or t <= 40/7; follow through on their equation, so allow t < their '64000/11200' as long as this value is greater than 5, since t=5 is one of the values given in the question). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
The curve C has equation x^2*tan(y) = 9,  0 < y < pi/2.
(a) Show that dy/dx = -18x/(x^4+81). (4)
(b) Prove that C has a point of inflection at x = the fourth root of 27 (x = 27^(1/4)). (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to differentiate tan(y) implicitly, tan(y) -> sec^2(y)*dy/dx (or an equivalent route, e.g. writing x^2 = 9*cot(y) or y=arctan(9/x^2) and differentiating). A1: Correct differentiation 2x*tan(y) + x^2*sec^2(y)*dy/dx = 0 (equivalent forms allowed, e.g. sec^2(y)*dy/dx = -18/x^3). M1: A full method to get dy/dx in terms of x alone, using sec^2(y) = 1 + tan^2(y) = 1 + f(x) (substituting tan(y) = 9/x^2, from the original equation, into sec^2(y)). A1*: Proceeds correctly to the given answer dy/dx = -18x/(x^4+81), with no errors. (4 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to differentiate the given first-derivative expression, using the quotient (or product) rule, to find d^2y/dx^2 (look for a correct attempt at [v*u' - u*v']/v^2 with u=-18x, v=x^4+81, u'=-18, v'=4x^3). A1: Correct, simplified d^2y/dx^2 = 54(x^4-27)/(x^4+81)^2, or equivalent such as (54x^4-1458)/(x^4+81)^2 (alternatively scores for showing that a correct unsimplified d^2y/dx^2 = 0 implies x^4=27, x = 27^(1/4), or for substituting x=27^(1/4) into an unsimplified but correct d^2y/dx^2 and showing it equals 0). A1: A correct explanation with a minimal conclusion and a correct second derivative - states that when x < 27^(1/4), d^2y/dx^2 < 0, and when x > 27^(1/4), d^2y/dx^2 > 0, giving a point of inflection at x = 27^(1/4) (can alternatively be argued via x^4 < 27, x^4 = 27, x^4 > 27, provided the conclusion states the point of inflection is at x=27^(1/4); or by substituting values either side of, and at, x=27^(1/4) into d^2y/dx^2, finding all three values, and making a minimal conclusion; a further alternative method finds d^3y/dx^3 and shows d^2y/dx^2=0 while d^3y/dx^3 != 0 at x=27^(1/4)). (3 marks)
questions.notes: The raw OCR text renders the fourth root of 27 as 'x = 4 27' with the root index and radicand run together (radical/index symbols are consistently lost in this dataset's extraction). This is confirmed against the mark scheme, where setting the second derivative's numerator to zero gives x^4 = 27, i.e. x = 27^(1/4).

questions.question_text: Prove by contradiction that there are no positive integers p and q such that 4p^2 - q^2 = 25. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
M1: For the key step in setting up the contradiction and factorising: assumes there are positive integers p and q such that 4p^2 - q^2 = 25, and factorises as (2p+q)(2p-q) = 25. M1: For deducing that, for p and q to be integers, either {2p+q=25, 2p-q=1} or {2p+q=5, 2p-q=5} must be true (award for deducing either of these statements; the case 2p+q=1, 2p-q=25 can be ignored as it cannot occur for positive p, q). A1: For correctly solving one of the given systems - for {2p+q=25, 2p-q=1}, candidates only need to proceed as far as p=6.5 to show the contradiction; for {2p+q=5, 2p-q=5}, candidates only need to find either p or q (p=2.5 or q=0), or alternatively state that 2p+q cannot equal 2p-q for positive integers p, q. A1: For a complete and rigorous argument covering both possibilities, with a correct conclusion that there are no positive integers p and q such that 4p^2-q^2=25. (4 marks)
Note: an alternative method sets q=2n+-1 (q odd) and expands to reach 4p^2 = 4n^2+4n+26 = 4(n^2+n)+26, hence p^2 = n^2+n+13/2, a contradiction since 4p^2 must be a multiple of 4 (equivalently p^2 must be a half-integer, so p cannot be an integer); this scores the same four marks for the equivalent steps.
